articles.title: Rob Brydon's battle to stay in character playing Peter O'Toole
articles.summary: Brydon stars in a new radio drama looking at the ups and downs of O'Toole's professional career.
articles.body:
Actor and comedian Rob Brydon has said it was difficult to stay in character while playing the role of a legendary actor portraying a man who was frequently too hungover to do his job.

He was speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme about his role in new radio drama, Peter O'Toole Is Unwell.

It encompasses O'Toole's critically acclaimed stage role in Jeffrey Bernard is Unwell in the West End in 1999, along with his universally panned performance of Macbeth in 1980.

Brydon, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, said taking on the role "felt like a challenge once we got into the studio" and he battled "to stay on the saddle" to remain in character.

The 61-year-old, known for his role as Uncle Bryn in Gavin and Stacey, said he initially thought "I could probably get close to his voice but there were a lot of words" written by award-winning playwright Terry Johnson.

The title of the audio drama is a riff on Keith Waterhouse's play Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell, in which O'Toole played the title role of journalist Jeffrey Bernard to rave reviews in 1999.

It is said to derive from the words used by The Spectator magazine when the journalist had missed the deadline to file his column.

In Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell, Bernard is accidentally locked in his favourite London pub overnight after falling asleep in the men's toilets.

He helps himself to a bottle of vodka and reflects on his colourful life.

Peter O'Toole Is Unwell is set in the actors dressing room in the Old Vic in London, where the actor performed in both Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell and Macbeth.

It is said to explore themes such as success, failure, love, ageing and the pain of coming to terms with who you really are.

Brydon said the play was a "wonderful script" based on the words of O'Toole from sources such as publications and memoirs, praising the "rhythm of his speech".

He said it was challenging "trying to get the essence of somebody else", adding that "it's as if you sort of drift... it was a constant battle to kind of stay in the saddle".

O'Toole was nominated for best actor in the Academy Awards on eight occasions, including for his portrayal of Wales-born army officer and writer TE Lawrence in 1962 film Lawrence of Arabia.

He was given an Academy Honorary Award for his entire body of work in 2003 and died aged 81 in December 2013.

Describing O'Toole as having "one of the most beautiful voices to listen to", Brydon said he found himself still speaking in his voice after recording it "and I would find myself thinking 'oh, I wonder how Peter would say that'".

Brydon said O'Toole's Macbeth did well on ticket sales "but only because people wanted to see it because they heard it was terrible".

"And then years later he's back in that same dressing room, and he was the talk of the town, the toast of the town, for Jeffrey Bernard [Is Unwell]," he added.

"It's a lovely dramatic device. So when he's there, doing Jeffrey Bernard, he's looking back at what he experienced with the Scottish play all those years ago."

Brydon said he loved the immediacy and intimacy of radio and had started out as a radio presenter on BBC Wales in the mid 80s, so it had "always been very special to me".

Brydon has also finished filming a new episode of The Trip with fellow actor and comedian Steve Coogan, where they play exaggerated versions of themselves .

The Trip is directed by Michael Winterbottom and follows the pair as they travel around the world and dine at different restaurants, visiting Scandinavia this time in The Trip to the Northern Lights.

"It's delightful, we get to have our cake and eat it really, because Steve Coogan and I play versions of ourselves and it's very bickering and very passive aggressive, or some of it is, other times just aggressive," he said.

Brydon said this was not the reality of their relationship, "but you just look for seeds of truth and exaggerate them for conflict and comic effect".

The Trip to the Northern Lights airs on Sky and NOW in December, while Peter O'Toole Is Unwell is now available on BBC Sounds.

articles.title: Israeli president picks Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu rival, to try to form government
articles.summary: Nov 7 () - Israel's president on Saturday chose Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's strongest rival, to try to form a new government following...
articles.body:
Nov 7 (Reuters) - Israel's president on Saturday chose Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's strongest rival, to try to form a new government following a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power.

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, is fighting ‌to stay in office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an October 27 election but still emerged as the ‌largest bloc in parliament.

Eisenkot, a former military chief, has declined to join forces with Arab parties, whose support would give him a majority of seats in parliament. But Arab leaders, incensed ​by what they view as the racist policies of Netanyahu and his far-right allies, still nominated Eisenkot to try to form a government first — giving him the most endorsements.

"President Herzog has invited Gadi Eisenkot to the President's Residence, where he will be tasked with forming the government tomorrow," said the spokesperson of President Isaac Herzog, whose largely ceremonial role involves nominating a candidate to form a coalition after elections.

In a post on X, Eisenkot wrote, "Now is the time ‌to form a national emergency government. I will do ⁠everything I can to ensure we are worthy."

EISENKOT FACES LONG-SHOT BID TO FORM GOVERNMENT

Weeks of protracted negotiations are expected to follow Eisenkot's nomination. He has 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

His potential ⁠pathways to power include trying to form a minority government with Arab party votes on key issues; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu.

Analysts say that all three options are unlikely to take shape. If Eisenkot fails, another ​candidate ​can try to form a government and if that candidate fails, parliament can nominate ​another. There is a deadline for the process of around ‌100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held.

Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu's wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority.

Eisenkot's Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.

A son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot, 66, would be the country's first prime minister from Israel's Mizrahi community, Jews who trace their roots ‌to the Middle East and North Africa.

Reserved and media-shy, Eisenkot only entered politics in ​2022. He briefly served in Netanyahu's wartime cabinet following Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on ​Israel before returning to the opposition.

From opposition, he publicly rebuked Netanyahu ​over his leadership, including his management of the military campaign in Gaza, and has sworn that he would not ‌serve in government with him.

Eisenkot's public standing is also bound ​up with the personal price his family has ​paid since 2023: a son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza.

Eisenkot highlighted his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his "Dahiyeh doctrine" of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel's 2006 war with Iran-backed Hezbollah in ​Lebanon.

Eisenkot has criticised settler violence against Palestinians, which has ‌surged since 2023, raising tensions in Israel's ties with Western states, and he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and ​Bezalel Smotrich, who have both faced sanctions by some Western countries for inciting violence against Palestinians.

(Reporting by Enas Alashray, Menna Alaa ​El Din and Alexander Cornwell; Editing by Cynthia Osterman and Timothy Heritage)

articles.title: Six killed in Krakow 'far-right' shooting, as three more bodies found in attacker's home
articles.summary: Police say the Polish attacker drove into a popular square in the city's centre and began randomly firing at people.
articles.body:
A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city.

Police said the attacker drove onto Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and began randomly firing at people.

The attacker, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, was injured in a gunfight with police, one of whom was critically injured in the process.

The 25-year-old Polish man - described by one minister as "ultra-nationalist" - has been taken to hospital for surgery.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said another three bodies were found during a search of the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away from Krakow.

Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man were the suspect's immediate family members.

He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

Four women and two men were killed in the square. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified, officials said.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today."

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

Images from the scene showed overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives.

Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight.

Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground.

The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground.

A Polish minister later said one police officer was fighting for his life and a second was expected to recover from a less serious injury.

Tusk later named them as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Morański - he said they "saved many lives" and called them "true heroes".

The gunman wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.

More weapons and ammunition were found in a car belonging to the suspect, whose name has not been confirmed.

Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultra-nationalist views".

Tusk vowed that any "possible supporters of the perpetrator" would be detained and appealed to the public for information.

A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere.

Of the 15 injured, two were police officers and five were foreign nationals - the interior ministry said they were from Britain, Austria, Russia, Germany and Portugal.

European foreign policy chief Kaja ⁠Kallas called it "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland."

British foreign secretary Ed Miliband said on social media the UK government "deeply mourns" those who died in the "appalling attack".

"All of my deepest condolences go to the families of the victims," he added.

The Foreign Office updated its advice after the attack and said people in the area should follow the advice of local authorities.

Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.

Cezary, a 24-year-old Polish university student in Krakow, said he did not realise the loud bangs he heard were gunshots until he saw four bodies lying on the street.

"We were still hearing gunshots, a lot of people were screaming," he said, adding that he saw someone trying to resuscitate a person covered in blood on the ground.

Caitlin Shasby, from Newcastle in the UK, said she heard shooting from her hotel room and was told to take shelter inside as police "barricaded" the street outside.

Another witness told Polish news website Inertia: "I saw shots being fired from the driver's side window and smoke was coming out.

"I ran to the police station in the main market square - when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor."

A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November.

articles.title: A former Las Vegas politician raised more than $70,000 to build a memorial for a slain police officer; prosecutors said she used the donations for rent and her daughter's wedding
articles.summary: A fundraising campaign intended to honour two Las Vegas police officers killed in the line of duty became the centre of a federal fraud case after more
articles.body: A fundraising campaign intended to honour two Las Vegas police officers killed in the line of duty became the centre of a federal fraud case after more than $70,000 raised from donors was spent elsewhere. Michele Fiore, a former Las Vegas city councilwoman who also ran as a Republican candidate for governor of Nevada, was convicted by a federal jury in October 2024. Prosecutors said she had assured contributors that every dollar would go towards building memorials for the fallen officers. Instead, the money went towards expenses unrelated to the project, including personal bills and political costs. The case raised questions about how donations collected in the name of public service were handled.Fiore assured donors every contribution would fund police memorialsFiore's fundraising efforts centred on plans to construct statues commemorating two Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department officers who had died while serving. At the time, she was a member of the Las Vegas City Council and used her public position to solicit contributions for the proposed memorials.The appeal was directed at people willing to support a project honouring officers who had lost their lives in the line of duty. Donors were given assurances that their contributions would be used entirely for the memorial construction. According to evidence presented during the trial, Fiore specifically represented that 100% of the money collected would go towards the statues.According to the US Department of Justice, the promise was an important part of the fundraising appeal. People contributing to the campaign believed they were helping establish permanent tributes to the officers rather than providing financial support for Fiore's personal or political activities. More than $70,000 was eventually collected. However, prosecutors said none of the charitable contributions was used to build the memorials.Where the donated money wentFederal prosecutors presented evidence that Fiore redirected the contributions towards expenses that had nothing to do with the proposed statues. The spending included political fundraising bills, payments towards her personal rent and money given to members of her family.The case also involved allegations that donations were used to cover expenses connected with her daughter's wedding. Rather than being kept for the memorial project, the money raised from supporters became a source of funding for private and political costs. The distinction between what donors had been told and how the money was actually spent formed the basis of the prosecution's case. The memorials, which had provided the stated reason for the campaign, did not receive any of the money raised.Federal jury convicts Fiore on seven fraud countsThe case went before a federal jury in the District of Nevada. In October 2024, jurors found Fiore guilty of one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and six counts of wire fraud. The verdict followed a trial in which prosecutors relied on court documents and evidence concerning the fundraising campaign and the subsequent use of the contributions. The charges related to the scheme through which donors were persuaded to send money based on representations about the construction of the police memorials. Fiore was 54 at the time of her conviction and was living in Pahrump, Nevada. Before the case, she had served on the Las Vegas City Council and had also pursued a campaign for Nevada governor.Fiore faces sentencing after conviction on federal countsThe final punishment was to be determined by a federal district court judge, taking into account the US Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory considerations. Those factors would help establish an appropriate sentence based on the offences and circumstances of the case. The Justice Department announced the conviction on October 4, 2024. Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Nicole M. Argentieri, who headed the department's Criminal Division, and FBI Las Vegas Special Agent in Charge Spencer L. articles.title: Labubu sales are slumping. Is the craze over?
articles.summary: Parent company Pop Mart's revenue has fallen as appetite for the quirky collectible monsters wanes.
articles.body:
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.

Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.

Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.

The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.

Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".

He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.

But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."

Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.

It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.

Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.

The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.

The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.

One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.

Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys . The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.

They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu .

A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find , with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.

Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.

Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.

For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.

"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.

Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.

Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.

As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.

Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.

Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.

"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year . "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."

Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.

That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.

Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.

But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."

After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular."

Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls.

His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles."

Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases.

"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out."

But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans.

Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines.

There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.

For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.

"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

articles.title: 'Child with cancer' stopped trick-or-treaters: What neighbourhood children did next left a mother overwhelmed
articles.summary: For every parent, Halloween is one of the sweetest moments of the year.
articles.body: For every parent, Halloween is one of the sweetest moments of the year. Dressing up their children in costumes, watching them go trick-or-treating and distributing candies to little visitors at the door, the festival brings back memories of their own childhood. For a moment, it seems to narrow the generation gap, allowing parents to relive the excitement of being a child through their little ones. But for one family in Atlanta, Halloween was going to be very different.The year was 2020. It was Halloween night, and children were rushing out into the streets wearing little costumes, going door to door, trick-or-treating. The neighbourhood was filled with the fragrance of freshly carved pumpkins and the crisp autumn air that welcomed the season. Amid all the festivities, there was one house that seemed unusual. No lights, no pumpkins, no decorations, as if the Halloween celebrations had passed this house by. There was nothing but a board outside that read: "Sorry, no candy. Child with cancer. See you next year!"This was the home of three-year-old Zoe Thomas, who was battling leukaemia, a type of blood cancer. Like every parent, her mother, Courtney Thomas, had probably imagined taking her little daughter out for trick-or-treating, dressing her up in the cutest costume and watching her collect candies from neighbours. But life had taken a different turn. With Zoe undergoing treatment and her immune system vulnerable, celebrating Halloween like other children was not an option that year.When leukaemia changed everythingAt just two years old, Zoe's life took an unexpected turn. Her mother, Courtney Thomas, first noticed something unusual while cuddling her daughter. As she rubbed Zoe's neck, she felt an odd swelling. Courtney, who herself worked as a paediatric nurse, was already concerned because Zoe had been unusually fatigued and was struggling with an ear infection. A few days later, her husband, T.J. Thomas, noticed tiny bruises near her collarbone. The couple took her to a paediatrician the following day, and blood tests confirmed their worst fears. Zoe had leukaemia.According to National Cancer Institute, USA, Leukaemia is a type of blood cancer that begins in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside our bones responsible for producing blood cells. It causes the body to produce large numbers of abnormal blood cells, which gradually crowd out healthy ones. This can affect the body's ability to fight infections, carry oxygen and prevent excessive bleeding or bruising.For Zoe and her parents, the diagnosis meant months of precaution, as treatments often left her immune system compromised to new infections, especially in 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic was on the rise. And so, when the Halloween arrives, her family decided to stay indoors with her daughter, to not make her feel alone when her friends were out there having fun collecting candies.When trick-or-treaters played a trickWhat happened was extremely unusual yet heartwarming. When the little ones passed by the house and saw the sign, instead of feeling sad and simply walking away, some of the neighbourhood children decided to do something rather unusual. They began leaving their own candies outside Zoe's home for her.One by one, children could be seen approaching the house, reading the message and placing their collected treats outside. Some even left little notes and messages of encouragement. The family's doorbell camera captured these unexpected acts of kindness, turning what was supposed to be a quiet Halloween night into something the Thomas family would remember for a long time.For these children, Halloween was usually about collecting as many candies as possible, but that night, they were willing to part with their own treats to bring a smile to a little girl they had never even met. It was a small gesture, perhaps, but for Zoe and her family, it meant much more than a bag full of sweets ever couldMaybe that’s what festivals mean. These small children understood how festivals should be celebrated. Halloween or any other festival is not just a day for partying and eating sweets; it's also a day to come together and celebrate.Maybe that is what festivals are really about. These little children understood something that often gets lost amid the celebrations. Halloween, or any other festival, is not just about partying, dressing up or collecting sweets. It is also about coming together, sharing what we have and making someone feel included.When Courtney saw what the children had done, she was overwhelmed. What began as a difficult Halloween for her family had turned into a reminder of the kindness and warmth that can exist within a community. For a mother who could only watch her little daughter miss out on the celebrations, seeing other children bring a little bit of Halloween to Zoe must have meant the world.You use AI every day. articles.title: Magnitude 5.7 earthquake hits central Japan, dozens injured
articles.summary: A strong earthquake of preliminary magnitude 5.7 struck central Japan early Sunday, prompting authorities to activate emergency response measures.
articles.body: A strong earthquake of preliminary magnitude 5.7 struck central Japan early Sunday, prompting authorities to activate emergency response measures. Japanese media reported that dozens of people were injured in the tremor.The earthquake struck at 1:04 am local time, with its epicentre in the western part of Shizuoka Prefecture at a depth of approximately 40 kilometres, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), as reported by Japanese daily The Mainichi.The tremor registered an intensity of upper 5 on Japan's seismic intensity scale in Chita City, Aichi Prefecture. Lower 5 intensity was recorded in parts of Aichi, Nagano and Gifu prefectures, indicating that the shaking was felt across a wide area of central Japan. Smaller aftershocks were also reported following the main tremor.Meanwhile, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi confirmed that strong shaking was recorded in Chita City and said there was no tsunami threat.Taking to X, Takaichi wrote: "At around 1:04 a.m. today, an earthquake struck with its epicentre in western Shizuoka Prefecture, and strong shaking with a maximum intensity of upper 5 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale was recorded in Chita City, Aichi Prefecture.""There is no risk of a tsunami," she added.The prime minister said the government had established a liaison office at the Prime Minister’s Office Crisis Management Centre to monitor the situation and coordinate its response."I have also directed efforts to assess the extent of the damage and provide accurate information to the public, and we are doing everything we can to respond," Takaichi said.Urging residents in the affected areas to remain vigilant, she added: "I ask everyone in areas that experienced strong shaking to remain alert to the possibility of another earthquake of similar magnitude."Authorities are monitoring the situation and assessing the extent of the damage, while residents have been advised to remain cautious amid the possibility of further tremors.You use AI every day. articles.title: Shah Rukh Khan reveals how father's death changed his sister's life, says his humour and flamboyance hide a deep sadness
articles.summary: For millions of people, Shah Rukh Khan is the man who can make them laugh, charm an audience with his words and turn even an ordinary moment into
articles.body: For millions of people, Shah Rukh Khan is the man who can make them laugh, charm an audience with his words and turn even an ordinary moment into something memorable. His humour, confidence and larger-than-life personality have become an inseparable part of his public image. But behind that familiar smile is a story of grief, loss and a childhood wound that he says never truly healed.In an unusually emotional conversation at Airtel THiNK 2012, the actor opened up about the death of his father, the devastating impact it had on his sister and the different ways the two siblings dealt with losing their parents.Recalling a moment that stayed with him for years, Shah Rukh spoke about watching his sister struggle after their father's death. He also made a deeply personal admission: much of the humour, flamboyance and constant activity that people associate with him may actually be his way of keeping sadness at a distance.The day his father's death changed his sister's worldRemembering the immediate aftermath of his father's death, Shah Rukh described how his sister reacted to the sudden loss. "I remember my sister standing in front of my father's dead body, and she just looked. She didn't cry, she didn't say anything. She just fell. And she hit her head on the ground," he recalled. What followed was even more difficult for the family. According to the actor, his sister did not cry or speak for nearly two years. He remembered her sitting and looking into space, unable to express what she was going through.The experience changed the family, but it affected his sister in a way that continued long after their father's death. Shah Rukh revealed that she had been highly educated and intelligent, having completed her MALLB, as he described it. She was everything their parents had hoped she would become. However, the sudden loss of their father made it extremely difficult for her to face reality. "She was highly qualified. She has done MALLB, very intelligent. Like my parents wanted her to be, but she could not face the reality of losing her parents," he said.When his sister was hospitalised during the making of DDLJThe actor also recalled how his sister's health deteriorated during the period when he was making one of the most memorable films of his career, 'Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge'. He revealed that she was hospitalised again during the film's making, and doctors told him that she might not survive. Faced with the possibility of losing his sister, Shah Rukh decided to take her to Switzerland for treatment. He arranged for her medical care there while he continued shooting the film's iconic song, *Tujhe Dekha To Yeh Jaana Sanam*."I took her to Switzerland and got her treated there while I was shooting Tujhe Dekha To Yeh Jaana Sanam," he recalled. Although her condition improved, the actor said she never completely recovered from the emotional impact of losing their father. The loss was further compounded when their mother passed away around 10 years later.Reflecting on their circumstances, he described himself and his sister using the words "Yatim and Yasim", explaining that they had become fatherless and motherless. For him, the loss was not simply about losing two parents. It was also about watching someone he loved struggle with grief in a way that changed the course of her life.Shah Rukh Khan admits his humour is a way of hiding sadnessPerhaps the most revealing part of the conversation came when Shah Rukh spoke about how he personally dealt with the same losses. While his sister became withdrawn and struggled to process the grief, he developed a different way of coping. He described it as a sense of detachment and false bravado. He suggested that the humour, confidence and flamboyance people often associate with his personality were not always expressions of happiness. In many ways, they were ways of keeping his own sadness from taking over."I somehow developed the sense of detachment, the sense of false bravado, which I show in public, a sense of humour, and a lot of things that I do, which people think is flamboyant and very Bollywood-like, to cover up the sadness affecting my life," he said. He explained that he constantly kept himself occupied, working around the clock, finding reasons to laugh and making jokes about situations in his life.For him, staying busy was more than a professional ambition. It was a way of protecting himself from falling into the same emotional state that he had witnessed in his sister. "So to avoid depression, I act," he admitted. He also made it clear that his constant drive was not simply about earning more money, becoming a bigger star or securing endorsements. There was something much more personal behind his need to keep going.A sister he loves and a pain he has never fully expressedDespite describing the difficult years his sister went through, Shah Rukh spoke about her with immense affection. He said that he loved her exactly as she was and considered her a much better person than he could ever be. He described her as a child of God, innocent and uncomplicated. He also shared that his children loved their aunt immensely, even more than they loved him and his wife. He was grateful that she remained such an important part of their family.However, he admitted that he did not have the courage to be as emotionally vulnerable as his sister. "I don't have the guts to be so simple, so hurt, so disturbed," he said. His words offered a different understanding of a personality that is often associated with confidence, wit and extraordinary energy. What audiences see as flamboyance, he suggested, can sometimes be a shield against feelings that are much harder to confront. Towards the end of the conversation, Shah Rukh acknowledged that it was perhaps the most honest he had ever been with anyone.The interview, originally from Airtel THiNK 2012, is a reminder that grief does not look the same for everyone. Some people withdraw into silence, while others keep themselves constantly occupied. Behind a public smile, there can be memories and emotions that remain difficult to put into words. And perhaps that is what makes this confession so moving. Shah Rukh Khan, a man who has spent much of his life making others smile, admitted that sometimes, his own smile was a way of keeping himself from breaking.You use AI every day. articles.title: From Ritual to Realisation: Why Celebrating Deepavali Every Year Means Ram Is Still Missing
articles.summary: Today we are celebrating Diwali. Shri Ram is coming home, and we are rejoicing.
articles.body: Today we are celebrating Diwali. Shri Ram is coming home, and we are rejoicing. We also commemorate this day as Shri Ram's homecoming after defeating Ravan. Burning effigies of Ravana, lighting lamps, and distributing sweets and gifts are all part of the celebration for children. The story of Diwali carries a true message - if we attain victory over the inner Ravana, which is the ego, then Shri Ram will come home. Home is your physical body. You listen to the stories, follow the tradition, but do not live by the message; getting that message is important. The real essence is for Shri Ram to enter the vessel of this physical body, whereas a concrete house contains only His idol. Do you seek Shri Ram in murti form, or the living Shri Ram who came to Ayodhya? Only one of the two, Ravan or Shri Ram, can remain; which is why it is called Advaita, nondual; and the play of Ravan and Shri Ram outside is Dvaita, duality. Duality is within you and outside as well; on the outside, you may appear noble and religious, but who are you on the inside? There is darkness and filth; the light of knowledge has never been lit. Ravan means the ‘i-ness’ that dwells inside you, ie, ego.Ravan was a supreme scholar; he let ego take over ten times, which is why he had ten heads. Do you perhaps have an ego regarding more than ten things? Therefore, wake up! Ravana died, but has your inner Ravana been destroyed—the one who takes pride in being a doctor, officer, minister, star, or wealthy person? When Ravan comes out, Shri Ram will appear inside as a form of consciousness. One who fails to manifest Him while alive will never meet Him after death. You may be the wealthiest tycoon, a minister, a celebrity, or a president, but the scriptures declare that you will face the punishments of the 8.4 million life forms; you could become a bug, a tree, a mountain, a bird, or an animal, but you will not find Shri Ram. When you approach death, a black body will come out as Ravana, and you are stuck in the cycle of birth and death; in other words, your human birth went in vain.On Deepavali, you light lamps and spread brightness, and you may do some cleaning, but if the trash of ego remains within, Shri Ram will not enter.The external Shri Ram is symbolic, asking us to keep Him in the garland of our breath, just as Hanuman tore his chest open to show his devotion that Shri Ram’s name beats within his heart. In Ayodhya, when Sita gifted a necklace of nine precious gems to Hanuman, he discarded it, asking, “Where is Shri Ram in this? What will I do with it?” When asked to show whether Shri Ram resides within him, he said that each breath recites Shri Ram as a rosary; he no longer needs an external rosary. When Shri Ram asked Him about his wish, he said, “My lord! If you want to grant me a wish, let it be solely this: to remain at your lotus feet eternally, in this life and beyond.” God said, “So be it” (tathastu), and that is why Hanuman is always found alongside Shri Ram today. Have you ever asked to remain at the lotus feet of Shri Ram for infinity?If you choose Shri Ram, then Ravana, i.e. ‘I’, gold, silver, bunglows, cars, wealth will not accompany you. You have to choose between the two; tell me, what will you choose? You have become a beggar for wealth. Ravan in the form of ‘i-me-mine’ has occupied all the space within. Thoughts of my home, my car, my family, etc, are always running through you. This is an artificial Deepavali that you are celebrating; the true Deepavali will be when Shri Ram manifests in you.Celebrating Deepawali year after year simply means Ram has not yet taken root in your heart; whoever truly embraces Ram never lets Him go. For them, every moment is Deepavali; they are not dependent on any specific day. It is Diwali and Shri Ram has arrived, but people worship Goddess Lakshmi expecting her to arrive. Goddess Lakshmi also laughs, watching people visit the temple and bow before Shri Ram's murti, yet ask me for material wealth like a bungalow or a car. Today is the day to wake up; we must.The unhappiness within is the biggest darkness; it is a dark moon night (amavasya). The flame of light is ready to be lit, but unfortunately, the bowl of ego clouds it. Once the barrier is lifted, the divine light appears. You may call this flame Goddess Lakshmi, Shri Ram, Shri Krishn, Guru Nanak Dev, Buddha, Mahavira, or Kabir.You are not this mortal body; awaken the flame of your true Self inside this mortal, clay physical body. It’s great that you are celebrating Deepavali. Have fun! Maya is to be enjoyed, but if you do not absorb its inner message and awaken the living Shri Ram within as inner radiance, then, in the end, one will be left with regret. Hence, wake up, or it will be too late.MAAsterG’s wisdom is available on his YouTube channels, ‘MAAsterG’ and ‘GOD HOME JOURNEY.'

articles.title: Diwali 2026 falls on November 8, a lucky date in Chinese culture: What the number eight teaches us about prosperity, food and the joy of sharing
articles.summary: Good fortune is what we share. This Diwali falls on a date Chinese culture would call lucky.
articles.body: Good fortune is what we share. This Diwali falls on a date Chinese culture would call lucky. The coincidence says something about how both traditions have always understood prosperity: as something set on a table, not stored in a vault.This year, Diwali falls on November 8. For most of us, that is simply a date circled for Lakshmi Puja. For anyone raised in Chinese tradition, it carries a greater significance. Eight is their luckiest number.I have always found it curious how cultures that never compared notes arrive at the same wish. In one, lamps are lit and doors left open so that prosperity can find its way in. In the other, a number is chosen with care, for a wedding date, a phone number, a shop’s opening day. Beijing opened the 2008 Olympics at 8:08 pm on the eighth day of the eighth month. Different rituals, the same emotion.A number that sounds like luckPart of the reason is linguistic. In Mandarin, eight, ba, sounds close to fa, a word tied to wealth and prospering. But the idea travels further than language. Buddhism’s Noble Eightfold Path is a route to a balanced life. Turn the numeral on its side and it becomes the symbol for infinity. Eight, in other words, was never only about money. It is about balance, and about good things that keep going and abundance.That, to me, is also the truest reading of Diwali. We pray to Goddess Lakhsmi, yes. But the festival does its real work at the door and at the table: the boxes of mithai carried across the city and meeting your loved ones.Luck, servedBoth traditions put their beliefs on a plate. In Chinese homes, dumplings are folded to resemble the gold ingots of old, long noodles stand for a long life, and fish is served because its name sounds like the word for surplus. Each dish is a wish you can eat.We do the same, perhaps less self-consciously. Sweets are the currency of Diwali goodwill. Festive meals pull three generations around one table. A recipe passed down is a family carrying its identity forward. The dishes change from across the country, but the instinct does not: abundance is something to be handed round.The table as translatorAfter a career spent in hotels and restaurants, I have come to believe the dining table is where these philosophies stop being abstract. People arrive for the food. What stays with them is the company, the discovery and the evening they had.It is also why, when we built a Pan-Asian restaurant at Bellona, we called it Eight. The name was a nod to prosperity, but the intent was balance: eight distinct culinary cultures, from Japan, China and Korea to Thailand, Vietnam, Burma, Malaysia and Indonesia, each allowed to keep its own character rather than being blended into one generic “Asian” menu. Japanese cooking prizes seasonality and precision. Thai food is a negotiation between sweet, sour, salty and hot. Chinese tables are built for sharing. These cuisines are as alike as they are different.Curiosity is the new festive moodI see this curiosity growing among guests. People want to know where a dish comes from, why an ingredient matters, and what a meal meant to those who first cooked it. Festivals are no exception. One family will gather over the same festive favourites it has eaten for decades. A group of friends might mark the same evening with a cuisine none of them has tried. Neither diminishes Diwali. Both are ways of celebrating the people in the room.That places a responsibility on my industry. Cultural storytelling cannot be a lantern hung for the season or a “festive special” printed on a table card. It has to show up in the authenticity of the cooking and the respect with which a tradition is handled. Borrowing a culture’s symbols without its substance is shallow and disrespectful.What we really wish forNone of this makes November 8 luckier than any other day. But the coincidence is a useful moment to ask what good fortune actually means. For some, it is a promotion or financial security. For others, it is good health, a happy home, or simply time with the people they love.The celebrations I remember best were never the most lavish. They were the ones with the longest conversations, the loudest laughter and a table with no room left on it.This Diwali, if the lamps and the number eight agree on anything, it is this. Good fortune is not only what we receive, it is what we share.Prashant Issar, MD of Bellona Hospitality and Founder of IshaaraYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Microdramas - why more Brits are watching these ‘snackable’ shows
articles.summary: The snappy, high-octane episodes - viewed on your phone - are huge in China and on the up in the UK.
articles.body:
Every evening, Heather Sharrock settles down to watch her favourite show.

But it's not on Netflix or iPlayer, or even on her television - it's on her phone.

And while some of us might get through a handful of episodes of our latest must-watch series every night, Heather can binge on dozens - because the 55-year-old from Scotland is into microdramas.

"There's so much rubbish going on in the world at the moment," Heather says. "It's just nice to switch off and not think for a little while."

Microdramas - already huge in China - are becoming increasingly popular in the UK, and can be found on apps like ReelShort, CandyJar and DramaBox. Last week, producers announced classic Neighbours storylines would be repackaged as super-short vertical episodes, one of the latest signs the format is moving into the mainstream.

Made up of snappy, high-octane episodes, they are usually 60 to 90 seconds long. Many focus on themes like forbidden love, family feuds and secret billionaires, and nearly every instalment ends on a dramatic cliffhanger. Each series tends to have 50 or more episodes, making the total runtime comparable to a feature film.

Diane Aitken, 45, a fan from Scotland, likens the werewolf- and vampire-themed microdramas she enjoys to 1980s US soaps Dallas or Dynasty "on steroids".

The shows emerged in China in the late 2010s as cheap and quick-to-film adaptations from online novels, says China-born filmmaker Samantha Sun, and for many fans they're a form of escapism.

Sarah-Jayne Lunn, 46, from Doncaster, says they helped her cope during a difficult period in her life. "Straight away I was hooked," she says. "I didn't have to overthink."

Jen Cooper, a microdrama viewer who now works as a consultant in the industry, agrees. She says microdramas were originally popular among middle-aged women looking for romance content, with many BookTok and romantasy devotees watching them, but they are are now popular with a much wider audience.

Last year, China's microdrama market was worth more than 100 billion yuan (£11bn) and viewer numbers surpassed 800 million, according to China's National Radio and Television Administration . But they're also big in South Korea, India and the US, with streamers including Prime, Peacock and Disney+ announcing plans to add microdramas to their services.

In the UK, TattleTV, which bills itself as the the country's first dedicated microdrama app, was launched earlier this year, while the Royal Television Society held an industry panel discussion on microdramas this summer.

Companies are also looking to capitalise on the buzz around microdramas, making branded short video ads for social media, with examples including productions from Jamie Oliver, the Co-op, and a Channel 4 and Sol de Janeiro collaboration.

'Snackable' shows you can have on in the background

Microdramas have to be fast-paced to keep viewers' attention, says Charlotte Brokenbrow of Welsh production company Spare Arrow, which made its first series this year.

"If you leave too much air in the script and in the video, then someone's going to get bored and will scroll on," she says.

As well as breakneck speed, microdramas have proved popular because people can watch them in bite-sized chunks, leading some analysts to describe them as "snackable".

They also feed into a shift towards "casual, low-commitment viewing that we can dip in and out of," says Dr Tina Kendall, associate professor of film and media at Anglia Ruskin University.

Some people told BBC News they watch them in the car while waiting to pick up their children from school, while others said they have one on in the background while they catch up on housework or admin.

It's so "obvious what's going to happen", Sarah-Jayne says she can even enjoy them while she is working.

Dedicated apps typically hook viewers by letting them watch the first few episodes for free, before then requiring a subscription. CandyJar costs £49 for one year, while DramaBox costs £110, but most microdrama apps allow binge-watchers to buy weekly subscriptions or watch ads in exchange for free episodes.

As you scroll through the apps, themes such as mafia bosses, enemies-to-lovers plotlines and cowboys recur.

Sun says Chinese production companies often replicate successful formulas, with only minor tweaks - and that's something Heather has noticed, too. "A lot of them have been the same story, just set in a different setting," she says, adding that she's now "fed up" seeing billionaire CEO storylines.

More outlandish titles include I Adopted My Stolen Baby, Craving My British Cowboy and Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas.

Some fans say they feel certain plots have been degrading to women, in some cases involving crude depictions of violence and sexual assault. "It became a bit of a sort of joke that the female actress has had a million hideous things happen to her and been crying and screaming 10 million times before she's even got to lunch," says Coco Taylor, an actress who starred in her first microdrama in 2024.

Taylor says she has turned down roles in some series because she felt they were too misogynistic . But she and many other microdrama fans say the storytelling has developed which they credit to more storylines now being written by US and UK teams, and they speak enthusiastically about microdramas branching out into genres such as comedy, thriller and horror.

Quick, cheap and 'financially attractive'

Haydn Wakeling, founder of production company Black Swan, first heard about microdramas earlier this year through a film industry contact. "Fast-forward to now and it's all anyone's talking about," he says.

Financially, microdramas are very attractive to directors and producers, Wakeling says - it typically takes less than two weeks to film a microdrama of between 60 and 90 minutes, pushing down costs.

Director Dan Löwenstein worked on his first microdrama, Mafia Lover, in February 2024. He's now on his 38th. Initially he worked on shows commissioned by Chinese apps, but says he's now working with US platforms, global streamers and UK companies, after the industry in China pivoted to AI production.

The UK is now Europe's largest audience for microdramas - and while many fans and producers in the industry are excited about the format's future, it's not without its critics.

Some deride microdramas as low-quality content that ruins people's attention spans. In an opinion piece for The Guardian , one writer said the shows were "catastrophically brainless and objectively bad".

But, as microdrama fan-turned-consultant Jen Cooper says: "No one's saying that this is profound, but if you've had that emotional reaction and you've made someone smile or made a hard day easier, then surely that is something wonderful to celebrate."

articles.title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.summary: While some believe the site should be partially or completely rebuilt, others want it abandoned and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
articles.body:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.

Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.

Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.

Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.

Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.

In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.

Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.

Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.

The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.

Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat

Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.

"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.

That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler committed suicide: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."

The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.

But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.

Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.

"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.

Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.

"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.

Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".

Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.

Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".

"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.

Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.

With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.

A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.

In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.

The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.

But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.

As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

articles.title: Duo-euthanasia: When your parents choose to die
articles.summary: Jan and Els sought medical intervention to end their lives together after 50 happy years of marriage, leaving behind their only child.
articles.body:
Some people might find this article upsetting.

Early one morning in June 2024, Bas pulled up next to his parents' campervan, parked on a sunny marina in the north of the Netherlands.

His father and mother, Jan and Els, had spent most of their married life on water. Now in their 70s, they could no longer manage a houseboat. Their campervan, positioned close to the yachts and dinghies, was the next best thing.

Jan and Els got into their son's car. Bas started the engine. This would be the final time he drove his parents anywhere. For Jan and Els, this journey - to the local hospice - would be their last.

At 10:30 that morning they would be administered lethal medication by doctors and die together in what is known in the Netherlands as duo-euthanasia. It's legal and it's rare, but every year more Dutch people choose to end their lives this way.

Three days before their fatal appointment at the hospice, Jan and Els gave an interview to the BBC in their campervan. Jan was living with continual pain, the legacy of years hauling cargo on the Netherlands' inland waterways. Els had been diagnosed with dementia. Their story was picked up and commented on around the world.

Now, more than two years on, the couple's only child describes trying to persuade his mother and father to delay their deaths while supporting their decision to stop living. He reveals the emotional burden his parents' decision placed on him and the profound loneliness that followed.

Bas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals.

"I still remember the whole trip," he says. His mum was in the back seat and his dad sat beside him. At first, they talked. Els seemed resolute about their decision to opt for euthanasia.

"My mum was convinced, certain about doing it," Bas says. "But my dad was a little bit emotional."

Jan asked his son if they were doing the right thing. Bas was thrown - he thought it would be his mum who might have doubts.

"My mum had always really enjoyed life," he says. "I remember she told me, 'I'd love to be 80 or maybe even 90 years old.'"

But his father had been talking about euthanasia for more than a decade because of all the years of pain.

In the car, Bas reassured his father. Once Jan calmed down, they drove without speaking, listened to music and watched the scenery go by.

In the months before the family made this journey, Bas had tried to persuade his parents to delay their deaths.

"I tried to convince them to stay a bit longer - why not wait until winter, or next year?"

Bas was conflicted. Although he thought his parents' decision to ask for euthanasia was the right one, he didn't want them to go.

"My dad, he was in this situation for 10 to 15 years, so he could probably have stretched it for another few years. But I think waiting for another year, then my mum would get into trouble…"

If Els delayed applying for euthanasia, she risked her Alzheimer's worsening, which might mean she would not be deemed capable of making the decision to end her own life.

"My dad said goodbye to my car - he liked my car, and he said, 'Good job', and 'thank you'.

"And then we walked inside," Bas says. "Imagine doing that - being in their shoes, taking that trip and that walk. It's so unreal."

For the next two hours, the couple's family and friends came and went. They reminisced, and listened to music. At one point, it crossed Bas' mind to call a halt to the proceedings.

"I had a feeling - 'OK, let's leave… Let's step into the car and drive away,'" he says. "But I didn't want to bring anything up that would make them feel uncertain - I had supported the whole [euthanasia] process.

"Better to keep everybody calm, and take the moment to say goodbye."

Just before 10:30am, doctors arrived to inject Jan and Els with the lethal medication that would kill them. The couple lay on hospital beds side by side. And in those final moments, before they lost consciousness, Bas witnessed his parents' closeness.

"I've seen them maybe three or four times in all my life walking hand in hand," he says. "But now they were laying there, hand in hand. And that gave me a really good feeling - they're really doing this together."

Bas describes that first half hour after his parents stopped breathing as "a factual thing" - they weren't alive anymore.

"Then you realise what the situation is - that's an unimaginable feeling."

In the hospice, sorrow hit Bas. He began to experience a profound loneliness.

"Grieving is a very, very deep thing to go through," he says, "and I don't have brothers and sisters - I really felt alone."

If we've been brought up by two parents, when the first dies, we can share our memories and sadness with the other as part of the process of bereavement. But Jan and Els were both gone.

"It was like my legs were cut off," remembers Bas.

His grief was physical too - he felt sick for four or five weeks. His body hurt.

"I would not really recommend this to others, and that's maybe a hard conclusion," he says. "It was maybe for them [my parents] the best option, but having lost them both at the same moment was very, very impactful."

Among people planning to apply for euthanasia in the Netherlands, especially those with dementia like Els, choosing the right moment to end your life may be complicated.

9,958 people in the Netherlands chose death by euthanasia in 2024

427 of those who chose death by euthanasia in 2024 had dementia - six had advanced dementia

108 people chose death by duo-euthanasia (54 pairs) that year

Source: Regional Euthanasia Review Committees (RTE)

As well as demonstrating they are suffering unbearably, they must be assessed by doctors as still having the capacity to decide for themselves they want to die. This can cause immense distress in dementia patients thinking about euthanasia, explains Dr Rozemarijn van Bruchem, a geriatrician and ethicist at the Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam.

"They think… I have that power right now, but now is too soon. But maybe next month is too late. So how do I decide at what point I need to start this process to see if I meet the criteria, to see if I can get euthanasia? And if I wait too long, might I have missed the window?"

Dr van Bruchem says it's because euthanasia is legal in the Netherlands that her patients experience this anxiety. And they know permission for an assisted death in cases of advanced dementia is rare. In countries where euthanasia is prohibited, like the UK, people with dementia may face many challenges, but they rarely have to weigh these life-or-death options - as Els did.

In 2024, she told the BBC that she and her husband couldn't wait because there was a chance her Alzheimer's would progress. And Jan was committed to dying with Els. He told the BBC that perhaps he was going too soon, but he had lived his life – his life was completed.

Jan and Els were very aware of the burden their end-of-life decisions placed on their son. Bas attended all the meetings his parents had with their separate doctors during the euthanasia process. There were open family discussions. Often, we have regrets when a loved-one dies – especially about what may have been left unspoken. This didn't happen to Bas. Two days before Jan and Els' appointment at the hospice on Monday 3 June he wrote them a letter.

"It was about eight pages," Bas says. "I went to the campervan late in the evening on Saturday night, two days before the event. I read the whole letter to them. It was about our lives, thanking them for what they'd done."

Jan and Els were deeply moved. And just as they rarely displayed affection to each other in public, they hadn't usually been demonstrative with their son either.

"You feel that they love you, but it's shown by doing stuff, not really saying it, or giving you a hug," says Bas. "My mum did [hug] more when she got dementia, but my dad never did – I never got a hug."

That changed in the campervan on that last Saturday night. Jan hugged Bas.

"He did it after that letter. It was maybe one of the best moments.

articles.title: Apple, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft’s $82 million donations come back to ‘haunt’ them as Democrats prepare to...
articles.summary: Days after winning control of Congress in the midterms, Democrats have picked their first big target: the tech giants that helped pay for President Donald
articles.body: Days after winning control of Congress in the midterms, Democrats have picked their first big target: the tech giants that helped pay for President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom. Senator Richard Blumenthal, who is set to chair the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has asked Apple, Google, Meta, Nvidia, Amazon and Microsoft to hand over records on their donations or face possible subpoenas.For now, the request is voluntary. That changes in January, when Democrats take the majority and gain the power to compel documents. Through two years in the minority, they had no such tool, and both the companies and the Trump administration largely ignored their requests.Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to reports in October, out of $333 million raised in private donations. Google directed $22 million to it from its settlement of Trump’s lawsuit over his YouTube suspension. Microsoft put in $10 million, as did federal contractors Lockheed Martin and Palantir.Big Tech’s Trump ballroom donations have been on the Senate’s radar for a yearBlumenthal first wrote to the donors in October 2025, soon after the East Wing was torn down to make room for the ballroom. That letter asked each company how much it gave, which administration officials it spoke to about the donation, and what lobbying contacts it had with the White House. The deadline to reply was November 7, 2025, exactly a year ago.His concern hasn’t moved since. Many donors, he wrote then, have “deep financial, business, or other personal interests” before the administration.The latest letters also went to Comcast, BlackRock, Cisco, Salesforce, HP, Micron, Caterpillar and Booz Allen, along with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen and former Marvel chief Ike Perlmutter. The tech companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.FCC chief Brendan Carr faces a November 30 deadline to hand over recordsBlumenthal’s letters did not stop at the tech firms. He also asked FCC Chair Brendan Carr for documents on the agency’s probes into media companies and its approval of the Paramount Skydance merger. He criticised Carr’s order for an early licence review of eight ABC stations owned by Disney too. Carr has until November 30 to start producing records, or the subcommittee will weigh “alternative measures” once Democrats take over.Over in the House, Representative Robert Garcia, set to chair the Oversight Committee, has named ballroom donors as an area of scrutiny as well. The companies now have until early January to decide whether they hand over the records by choice or wait for a subpoena.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
