articles.title: As fresh peace talks loom, Putin is escalating his efforts to shatter Ukraine’s economy
articles.summary: As Russia struggles to advance on the battlefield in eastern Ukraine, it continues to pour more resources into the war in the skies. Russian missiles and drones are hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure harder and earlier in the year than in previous years, analysts say, and the Kremlin has broadened its targets to further damage the Ukrainian economy.
articles.body: As Russia struggles to advance on the ground in eastern Ukraine, it is pouring more resources into the war in the skies. Russian missiles and drones are hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure harder and earlier in the year than in previous years, analysts say, and the Kremlin has broadened its targets to further damage the Ukrainian economy. An independent United Nations investigations panel last week concluded that Russia committed war crimes and crimes against humanity by intentionally attacking civilian infrastructure, particularly with attacks on vital energy systems during the severe winter of 2025-2026. This winter, experts say attacks are expected to be worse. With the US set to mediate in fresh peace talks next week, Russian President Vladimir Putin is only escalating his attacks on Ukraine. The Russian air campaign is now “clearly aimed at destroying the Ukrainian economy,” said John Lough, head of international partnerships at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a London-based think tank. Lough also told CNN that he believes many of Kyiv’s allies in Europe haven’t grasped “just how serious this situation is that is developing in Ukraine,” nor how much financial burden it could place on European partners. “Putin has concluded that he can’t win in Donbas by committing more men to battle and trying to push forward, because the Ukrainians have actually had a relatively successful summer,” Lough said. “(Putin) has concluded the only way to break that is to actually break the economy, and they are doing that in a systematic way.” Cristian Vlas, an Eastern Europe researcher at ACLED, a global conflict monitor, said, “We’ll see a terrible humanitarian situation this winter and much earlier than last year.” “It’s not going to be a winter as usual,” he told CNN. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest since the first months of the war, with Russian strikes killing more than 2,700 Ukrainian civilians so far in 2026, according to data compiled by ACLED. The number of Russian strikes launched on Ukraine has increased steadily in 2026. In January 2026, there were 3,650 Russian strikes on Ukraine. For October, that figure increased to 5,532. Ukraine’s attacks inside Russia have also increased, with 2,302 strikes carried out in October. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said it hit at least Russian seven enterprises involved in weapons production, three military airfields and key radar and military communications facilities last month. This summer, Ukraine also launched attacks on the warehouses of Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries. Russia targets industry, grain exports Russian attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea exports, Danube River ports, industrial warehouses, railway infrastructure and steel industry are now frequent events. Some of that infrastructure has both civilian and military purposes, but experts said that recent attacks have brazenly targeted civilians alone. At least 55 Ukrainians were killed Monday when Russia bombed a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia, one of the deadliest incidents of a conflict in its fifth year. Moscow consistently denies targeting civilians. Major Ukrainian steel plants in Kryvyi Rih and Zaporizhzhia were hit in ballistic missile strikes between August and October, forcing them to shut down. The city of Kryvyi Rih has raised the alarm about “serious socio-economic consequences” and loss of income for thousands of families due to the steel plant closure. “Those are hits to Ukraine’s tax base, not just you know ‘industry’ in a very abstract manner,” Vlas said. “It hits at the people’s salaries.” Combined with Russian strikes on other major sectors like agriculture and grain exports, Vlas noted that it appears to be an effort by Moscow to create multiple economic firestorms across Ukraine’s economy at the same time. “They’re targeting things like malls, storages, warehouses – so, that disrupts the flow of goods, the sale of goods, and so on,” said Kateryna Stepanenko, the Russia Team Lead at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington think tank that closely monitors the conflict. And while Russia once mostly attacked at night, Stepanenko said that it has been increasingly conducting daytime strikes, which are partially aimed at upending day-to-day business activities in Ukraine. “What that does is that it activates an air alert under which many Ukrainian government buildings or businesses cannot legally operate, and so that disrupts business,” she told CNN. Strikes on energy infrastructure also disrupt economic activity, given that power and water outages severely impact businesses. Russian forces have also started to hit energy infrastructure in areas of Ukraine that were not previously targeted, such as the western city of Rivne, said Stepanenko, which creates new challenges for Ukraine’s threadbare air defenses. The impacts of energy strikes are mounting. Many of Ukraine’s power stations are damaged beyond repair. “We just have to keep in mind the cumulative effect of this war, and the very great fatigue on the Ukrainian side,” Lough said. “With the fabric of the economy strained in this way, it’s really a very dangerous moment.” Local authorities in Kyiv said that roughly 40% of buildings didn’t have heating as of Saturday. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha gave yet another stark warning this weekend, as the first snowfall of the year arrived in Ukraine. “Moscow is deliberately seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without electricity, heating, and water as winter approaches,” Sybiha said. “Russia is trying to achieve through cold and darkness what it cannot achieve on the battlefield.” Civilians paying the price The higher civilian casualties come as Russia has expanded its use of jet-powered Shahed drones and loitering munitions – weapons that are difficult for Ukrainian forces to shoot down. Ukraine is working to improve its interception capabilities for both, but at the moment, experts said, the Russian weapons have an edge. Ukraine is also dealing with a persistent shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, which are one of the few defensive weapons that can take down a Russian ballistic missile. As a result, “the civilian fatalities and casualties have been increasing almost since April, almost constantly. But the surge in fatalities in October – early October – is just staggering,” ACLED’s Vlas told CNN. Civilians are also paying a high price. A new report from the International Rescue Committee (IRC) found that in southern and eastern regions of Ukraine, financial distress is pushing civilians to abandon their homes or take grave risks to keep making money. For example, in some regions, IRC found that farmers were risking their lives to work on land contaminated with mines, just so they could retain some source of income. Among hundreds of households surveyed in the region of Mykolaiv, 91% said they were in urgent need of financial assistance. In Dnipropetrovsk, 42% cited financial assistance as an urgent need. “The lack of financial resources is not just (about) paying the bills. It really creates the pressure to make the life-changing decisions,” said Olga Kashuba, IRC’s deputy director of field management in Ukraine. And for many civilians in eastern Ukraine, the conflict began disrupting their lives and livelihoods in 2014, she noted, meaning they have suffered more than a decade of economic pressure. Based in Kyiv, Kashuba herself has witnessed the growing economic anxieties and the loss of neighbors’ incomes. Her local farmers’ market closed down after it was destroyed in a Russian strike. A nearby warehouse was hit in another recent attack, damaging the inventory of multiple small booksellers, she told CNN. “When the grocery shops are burned, when the warehouses are burned… yes, it affects the goods,” Kashuba said. “But also, this is the source of income for a number of people – for thousands of people.” CNN’s Becky Pinnington, Kosta Gak and Victoria Butenko contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Will never visit Ram Temple': TMC's Kirti Azad invokes Sita's Agni Pariksha in attack on BJP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress MP Kirti Azad on Sunday hit out at the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) over its repeated references to the Ram Temple, accusing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress MP Kirti Azad on Sunday hit out at the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) over its repeated references to the Ram Temple, accusing the party of using religious sentiments for political gains. He said he had visited the Kamakhya Temple but had never visited the Ram Temple in Ayodhya and had no intention of doing so in the future.His remarks come amid a political row over Samajwadi Party (SP) supremo and former Uttar Pradesh chief minister Akhilesh Yadav's proposed visit to the Ram Mandir and Hanumangarhi temple in Ayodhya on December 12.The proposed visit has drawn criticism from the BJP, which has termed it a political exercise ahead of the elections and accused Yadav of seeking electoral mileage through visits to prominent religious sites.Speaking to news agency IANS, Azad questioned why the BJP repeatedly invoked the Ram Temple and accused the party of misusing temple donations."I do not understand why this Bharatiya Janata Party, which is involved in extortion and stealing donations, keeps talking about the Ram Temple. I have not visited the Ram Temple; I have visited the Kamakhya Temple. Are they suggesting that a person is not a Hindu if they worship Goddess Kamakhya? I worship Goddess Kamakhya, but I have not visited the Ram Temple," he said.Referring to Goddess Sita's birthplace and the episode of her Agni Pariksha, Azad questioned the circumstances surrounding her subsequent abandonment."I belong to the birthplace of Mata Sita. Mata Sita had to undergo the Agni Pariksha, and even after passing it, she was abandoned. Is it right for any human being to treat his wife this way -- to make her undergo the Agni Pariksha and then abandon her even after she passes it? This is not right. I visit Kamakhya Temple and Tripura Sundari Temple. Does that mean I am not a Hindu?" the TMC MP said.Reiterating his stand, Azad told IANS, "I have not gone to Ram Temple, nor will I ever go. I'll go to Mathura."He further accused the BJP of exploiting religious sentiments for political purposes and said the party had failed to establish the ideals of Ram Rajya in the country."They are doing this for politics and are orchestrating robberies and thefts at every temple. They do not have any other issue than Ram. The BJP has not brought Ram Rajya but Ravan Rajya in the country," he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Hundreds of seagrass shoots found in Cornwall estuary
articles.summary: There were fears a restoration trial may not succeed when only six seedlings had emerged in April.
articles.body:
More than 430 seagrass shoots have been discovered in the Fowey Estuary, giving conservationists hope that one of the UK's most important marine habitats can be brought back to Cornwall's waters.

The new growth was recorded across 50 patches of seabed during summer surveys carried out by Cornwall Wildlife Trust.

The findings come despite fears the restoration trial might not succeed when only six seedlings had emerged by the end of April.

Chloe James, of Cornwall Wildlife Trust, said the shoots were "hugely encouraging" after an "uncertain start to the spring".

Volunteers collected seagrass seeds from a donor meadow in Torpoint in autumn 2025 before planting them in the estuary. The seeds remained buried through the winter before beginning to grow in spring.

"The new growth is a powerful reminder of why restoration work takes time, persistence and a willingness to keep learning," said James.

Earlier work involved some of the trust's first attempts to restore seagrass meadows in Cornwall's estuaries, with volunteers collecting and planting thousands of seeds while researchers tested different restoration methods.

Seagrass, which may not look remarkable, is often described as the sea's equivalent of a woodland, said the trust.

It provides shelter and nursery grounds for fish and other marine life, helps improve water quality, locks away carbon and reduces coastal erosion.

The trust said mainland Britain had lost up to 92% of its seagrass meadows over the last century. Previous research highlighted by the project found seagrass could capture carbon up to 35 times faster than tropical rainforests.

The restoration effort has not been without setbacks. In the Helford Estuary, algal growth appeared to wipe out planted seedlings at one site, although three plants were later found to have survived and had started spreading.

More seeds are due to be planted in the Fowey Estuary and Helford Estuary, with further monitoring planned for spring 2027.

articles.title: Canadian contractor billed a woman $778 for visiting her summer cabin to quote a propane fridge installation; tribunal dismissed his claim after she refused to pay
articles.summary: Vernon contractor Aslan Electrical, Plumbing, Gasfitting, Refrigeration and Sheetmetal Services, billed a customer $778 for a site visit meant to produce
articles.body: Vernon contractor Aslan Electrical, Plumbing, Gasfitting, Refrigeration and Sheetmetal Services, billed a customer $778 for a site visit meant to produce a quote for a propane fridge, then took her to the online small claims court when she refused to pay. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal dismissed the claim in its entirety, finding no binding contract existed and that the customer reasonably expected a free site visit, since no evidence showed she was told of any charge. A second decision issued the same day went the contractor’s way, showing that signed work orders and clearly stated charges matter here.A request for a propane fridge quote at a summer cabin ended with a surprise $778 invoiceAccording to iNFOnews, Melanie Moore asked the company for a quote to install a propane fridge at her summer cabin. A technician visited and some time later phoned her with a price. Moore found it was more than she had budgeted for and decided not to go ahead.The company later sent her a bill. It covered five and a half hours of labour and $71 for driving 75 kilometres, plus tax and parts. Moore told the tribunal she had understood the visit was only to prepare an estimate and did not expect to be charged for it. She was also confused about the labour, because the technician had been at her property for less than an hour.Before any legal action, Moore offered to pay for one hour of the technician’s time to settle the matter in good faith. The company turned that offer down and took her to the tribunal instead.The contractor said she agreed to the job on the phone, but the call recordings told another storyAslan argued that Moore agreed to hire it for the installation while speaking to its dispatcher, then cancelled once she heard the price. It said it should still be paid for the time and expenses it put into the job. The case turned on whether a written or verbal contract existed, either for the installation or for the quote itself.The company submitted two audio recordings of calls between Moore and its dispatcher. In them, Moore asks for a price, and the dispatcher says they have no idea, because invoicing is not their area. They then discuss the cabin’s location and arrange a visit. The tribunal ruled that no contract was formed during the phone call.The tribunal found Moore reasonably expected a free visit and could decline the work over priceBecause the dispatcher could not discuss price and instead sent a technician, the tribunal said Moore reasonably believed the cost would be settled on site, and that she could refuse the work if she disagreed with the quote. Moore said she had made clear she wanted to know the cost before committing. Evidence backed this up: the technician’s own note on the file described the aim as producing a rough estimate.Aslan then argued that it had a call-out charge, billed from the moment the technician left the shop until the return. The tribunal found no evidence the company had told Moore this. It said it was reasonable for her to assume a technician was being sent to look at a possible job free of charge, and it dismissed Aslan’s claim in full.Before the ruling, the contractor had been involved in 45 tribunal cases in five yearsThe company was already a familiar name at the tribunal. In the first weeks of 2025 alone, it had taken six clients to the online small claims court. Over the previous five years, it had been involved in 45 tribunal cases and more than 60 cases in the British Columbia Provincial Small Claims Court.A separate ruling the same day ordered another customer to pay for diagnosing a leaking water pipeNot every dispute went against the company. In a separate decision issued on 20 February, 2025, Aslan sued customer Judy Knott over a $527 unpaid bill. The company first visited her home in 2021, fixed her air conditioner and billed $233.A year later, it returned twice to assess a leaking water pipe outside her property and recommended replacing 12 feet of pipe. Knott declined the work, and the company billed two hours at $294. She told the tribunal she had been under the impression there would be no charge, or a very small one, since the company had not done anything for her.The tribunal ruled that Aslan had been clear about the charge for diagnosing the problem and that Knott had signed the work order. It ordered her to pay $752, covering the two unpaid bills plus fees and interest.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: She began with a fundraiser to feed just 25 schoolchildren; today, Kenyan entrepreneur Wawira Njiru employs 6,000 people, and her organisation serves 730,000 children every day
articles.summary: William Wordsworth wrote, “That best portion of a good man's life, His little, nameless, unremembered acts of kindness and of love.” And sometimes, it
articles.body: William Wordsworth wrote, “That best portion of a good man's life, His little, nameless, unremembered acts of kindness and of love.” And sometimes, it might seem that these acts are all for nothing. But just as the darkest night gives way to the brightest dawn, small acts of kindness that people often ignore can turn into something beyond imagination. That's what happened with Kenyan entrepreneur Wawira Njiru, who started feeding 25 schoolchildren as a small act of kindness. Who knew this little initiative would turn into something so massive?How a small fundraiser for 25 children beganWhile studying nutrition in Australia, Njiru began thinking about the children growing up in her home country, Kenya, who struggled to get proper meals. She decided to do something that many people only think about. When she realised that some of her university friends had money to spare and wanted to contribute towards a cause, she started her first fundraiser in 2010. With the money she collected, she established a small kitchen in Ruiru, Kenya, in 2012, where meals were initially prepared for just 25 children.Njiru's idea was simple: provide children with nutritious meals so that hunger would not stand in the way of their education. But running a school kitchen was only the beginning. As more people became involved and the initiative expanded, what had started as a small community effort gradually developed into Food4Education, an organisation working to make school meals accessible to children across Kenya.But how did a small kitchen started by a few people become so massive?How Food4Education grew into a massive school-feeding initiativeAs the number of children grew, Njiru and her team realised that the initiative needed more than just goodwill and donations to sustain itself. They began building a system that could prepare and distribute meals to growing numbers of children without compromising on quality. In 2016, the organisation established its first central kitchen, with the capacity to prepare meals for 10,000 children. It later expanded its operations across different parts of Kenya, opening larger kitchens and building partnerships with schools and local authorities.One of its biggest developments came in 2019, when Food4Education introduced its Tap2Eat system. Using digital wristbands, children can collect their meals by simply tapping their bands, while parents can contribute towards the cost through the system. The technology also helps the organisation track meals served and manage its operations more efficiently. Rather than making school lunches entirely dependent on donations, the model allows parents to contribute a small amount towards their children's meals, with additional support coming from government programmes and donors.The organisation has also built connections with local farmers, sourcing around 80% of its food from small-scale agricultural producers. This not only helps provide fresh ingredients for school meals but also creates a steady market for farmers. Today, Food4Education has grown into an organisation employing more than 6,000 people, with operations reaching over 2,700 schools and providing more than 700,000 meals daily, according to its official figures.Wawira Njiru's vision and the impact of her workFor Njiru, however, the work is far from over. She wants to take the school-feeding model beyond Kenya and make nutritious meals a more accessible part of children's education across Africa. Her organisation is also working towards reaching one million children every day by 2027. The idea is to build a sustainable system in which schools, governments, farmers and communities can work together to address childhood hunger rather than treating it as an isolated problem.Her work has also received international recognition. In 2026, Njiru received the German Africa Prize for her contribution to tackling food insecurity and improving children's access to education. From a small fundraiser that began with just 25 children to an organisation employing thousands of people and feeding hundreds of thousands every day, her journey shows how a local initiative can grow into something with a much wider social impact.Ultimately, what began as an effort to put food on 25 children's plates has become a reminder that meaningful change does not always require a grand beginning. Sometimes, it simply requires someone to take the first step.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Rent-a-grandchild: Businesses offering companions to elderly grow in India
articles.summary: A small but growing number of firms selling what families once took for granted: someone to take care of the seniors.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – Both daughters of S Budhiraja live in the United States. Yet, when he and his wife head out to the market in Gurugram, a bustling business district on the outskirts of India’s capital, a young man walks beside them.

It is 26-year-old Roney Raju, their “hired grandson”.

Across Indian cities, a small but growing number of companies are now selling what families once took for granted: someone to take care of ageing people. Chores include taking them to the temple, sitting with them during a hospital visit, playing cards, or simply listening to them.

Some firms call such workers “children for hire”; others call them a “grandchild for rent”.

India, the world’s most populous country, is growing older quickly.

People over 60 made up 10.5 percent of its population in 2022, a demographic projected to nearly double to 21 percent by 2050, according to the India Ageing Report 2023 by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the International Institute for Population Sciences.

That means about 347 million elderly Indians – a number almost equal to the entire population of the US, the world’s third most populous nation – will need specialised care by 2050.

Several Indian startups see the opportunity, with the Indian government estimating the senior care industry at about $7bn.

Raju, holding a master’s degree in social work, works for one such company in Gurugram. He has been looking after the Budhirajas for the last few months.

“I was comfortable with him from the get-go,” Budhiraja, who is in his 80s, told Al Jazeera. “I feel he understands me 200 percent.”

Raju describes the bond in the same vein. “Right now, he is family to me,” he said. The couple, he said, see him as “their proxy child, and much more than a service companion”.

The bond has deepened over the past months. When Budhiraja was admitted for surgery, Raju kept track of the doctors and the medicines. He would even call to check on them after his shift had ended.

Raju’s boss Gaurav Mittal says many clients actually come to treat their companions “like their own grandchildren”.

He charges 450 rupees ($5) an hour for 10 hours of service in a month, or 400 rupees ($4.5) per hour if it is 25 hours. Like a mobile phone recharge, unused hours are rolled over to the next month.

In a country with an average per capita income of about 220,000 rupees ($2,750) a year, Mittal’s service caters to a small minority of urban, financially secure families.

Mittal said the idea for his company came from home. After his father died four years ago, his mother had to leave their hometown and move in with him. She was sociable and had money to spend, but depended on family members to go anywhere.

“The world is not designed keeping the senior citizens as the central pillar,” Mittal said.

The idea for such startups, however, is not entirely new.

A 2017 report counted at least five startups offering young companions to seniors. In 2022, the late Ratan Tata of the Tata Group promoted a Mumbai-based startup whose tagline says: “Everything Grandkids Do!”

The companions who work for these companies undergo police verification before they start working for a senior person. Before working alone, they often shadow a senior staff member on home visits.

Most companions are trained in psychology, social work or hospitality.

Vinay Kumar works as a companion for a firm based in the southern city of Hyderabad.

“We are not just taskmasters, but we develop a relationship with our clients. We support them and spend quality time with them so that they don’t miss their close ones,” he told Al Jazeera. “They may still do, but we try.”

The 2023 United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) report projects that older Indians will outnumber the country’s children by 2046. And many of these seniors are lonely.

In 2022, India conducted the Longitudinal Ageing Study, a national survey of more than 72,000 people. It found that 20.5 percent of middle-aged and older adults reported moderate loneliness, while 13.3 percent categorised their loneliness as severe.

Among people over 60 who lived alone, more than a third (37 percent) reported feeling lonely, the study found.

Globally, a study commissioned by the World Health Organization in 2025 found that loneliness affects one in six people and is linked to about 871,000 deaths a year.

Santosh Abraham, CEO of a Bengaluru-based startup founded in 2015, says while the children of elderly people are worried about medical emergencies or market errands, their parents mostly had a different concern.

“I am lonely, I don’t have anyone to talk to,” Abraham recalled one of his clients as saying. “I have done so much for my family and society; there is no recognition for it.”

Abraham said the most common request he gets is one that “nobody says out loud”.

“A senior calls us claiming to feel unwell. A care manager arrives, finds nothing wrong, and is then asked to sit and talk for an hour,” he said. “They just want company.”

Kumar said companions like him have to “understand their pain”.

“Most of the seniors who are living alone are very lonely. They want someone to play cards or indoor games with. Someone wants to go to a movie, or a temple, or parks, or attend local programmes,” he said.

Abraham said some seniors find a stranger easier to confide in. “With a companion, there is no baggage,” he told Al Jazeera.

For the young people doing the work, the line between their job and a relationship blurs quickly.

Raju says the visits to the Budhirajas are harder than office work. “Forming an emotional connection is never easy and is different each and every time,” he said.

Kumar, in Hyderabad, agrees. He said his clients often tell him about health problems that they hide from their children living in another city or abroad so as not to worry them.

He recalled a client who went from shutting the door on his face because he did not know English or Hindi to paying for his driving lessons and introducing him to people as his “god-gifted son”. When the man died in 2023, his son asked Kumar to perform the final rites alongside him.

Kumar once even cut short his 12-day marriage leave because one of his clients kept calling, asking him to come. “I genuinely feel these seniors are my own parents and grandparents,” he said.

Others are more cautious about what the job demands.

Prashanth Reddy, founder of the Hyderabad-based company that Kumar works for, said companions must understand boundaries.

“Companions are there to provide support, not to replace doctors or mental health professionals,” he said.

Abraham agreed. He said he underlines one golden rule during his training sessions with aspiring companions: “Talk less and listen more.”

The children of such elderly people who buy the services of these companies say paying takes out the awkwardness of asking neighbours or relatives for help.

“When you pay for a service, you don’t have to feel like you’re asking someone for a favour,” says Vinnay K, a US-based software professional, who has been hiring a companion for his ageing mother for five years.

Shilpa Bandyopadhyay, assistant professor at Jindal Institute of Behavioural Sciences near New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that hiring a companion “should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that their families have failed”.

She said a growing demand for professional elderly care raises harder questions about a family-centric society like India’s.

“Do we recognise ‘companionship’ as a legitimate and continuing need of our older family members or see eldercare mainly as food, shelter, healthcare and physical help?” she asked.

She argued for “a more balanced ecosystem of ageing” that brings together families, community networks, accessible public spaces and affordable professional services, without romanticising traditional family structures or dismissing new ones.

“At the end of the day, the question isn’t who lives with an older person,” she said, but “rather whether the older person feels seen, heard, safe, valued, and meaningfully connected”.

Back in Gurugram, Budhiraja is asked how he would feel if Raju did not show up for work tomorrow.

“I will make sure he comes after finding out why he couldn’t come,” he said. “I need him. As you grow older, the needs are more.”
